transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-13
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Ramos (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Talon - Head of ML), Samir Patel (Talon - Platform Engineer), Lena Ortiz (Talon - CTO)

Summary:
Short discovery focused on Talon's latency and throughput requirements for payment fraud detection and realtime scoring. Customer currently evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for p95 targets under streaming and high-concurrency token generation. Agreed to run joint benchmarks and share security docs.

Topics covered:
- p95 latency targets for single-turn and streaming responses
- concurrency and qps expectations (peak and steady)
- token/sec benchmarking methodology and metrics to capture (p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU util, batch sizes)
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs: predictability, cost, isolation
- Networking and security requirements (VPC peering, SSO/SAML, KMS)
- Next steps: benchmark run, pricing, follow-up deep dive

Action items noted in call (see metadata): Miguel to prepare runbook, Sofia to send pricing and configs, Aisha to confirm infra availability.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Sofia: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm sofia from redwood, i'm the AE on this account, miguel from infra will jump in on the latency bits, hows it going?
[00:06] Aisha: hey sofia, yeah good thanks. lena and samir on also, just here to walk through our requirements and see where redwood fits.
[00:12] Samir: hi, quick note from me: we're very sensitive to p95 for fraud scoring, want to keep it below ~200-250ms for single-turn decisions, streaming for live session risk scoring can be slightly higher.
[00:24] Miguel: ok that's helpful, couple clarifying q's — when you say single-turn are we talking typical prompt length? tokens?
[00:30] Aisha: yeah single-turn is short prompt, 40-120 tokens, basically model returns a single classification or small json payload. average payload size is 60 tokens returned.
[00:42] Miguel: great. are you planning to use streaming for anything else besides live scoring?
[00:47] Lena: mainly live scoring for checkout flows, and some merchant support chat where we want a streaming feel. but the critical SLA is fraud/ml scoring at checkout.
[00:56] Sofia: and what's your concurrency target — like both steady state and burst?
[01:01] Samir: steady is around 200 concurrent requests, bursts up to 1k for Black Friday style events. throughput-wise we aim 1500-2k reqs/sec at peak, but those are small token sizes so tokens/sec is low per request, still high QPS.
[01:15] Miguel: okay so small responses but high qps; that's where batching and autoscaling matter. redwood hosted can handle bursts, but dedicated gives more predictable p95 under sustained high-concurrency.
[01:29] Aisha: can you unpack that — what kind of p95 differences have you seen between hosted and dedicated?
[01:34] Miguel: from our benchmark baseline: for comparable model variant, hosted p95 under multi-tenant peaks can vary 10-30% higher than dedicated due to noisy neighbors and autoscaler cold starts. with dedicated provisioning and right batch tuning we've seen p95 single-turns ~120-220ms on A100-style fleet for 60-token responses at 200 concurrency.
[01:55] Samir: that's promising. what about streaming — we need p95 for first-token latency under 150ms ideally, and steady token throughput for the stream of about 30-40 tokens/sec per session.
[02:08] Miguel: streaming is trickier, first token latency depends heavily on prefix KV cache warmness and network path. on dedicated with warm cache we can hit first-byte p95 ~90-140ms. hosted sometimes is 150-250ms depending on load.
[02:21] Aisha: how do you measure tokens/sec? we use tokens/sec and end-to-end p95 as our main metrics.
[02:26] Sofia: good question — our SEs recommend measuring: p50/p95/p99 for end-to-end latency, tokens/sec sustained over 60s windows, GPU utilization, batch sizes that occurred, and tail latencies per shard.
[02:37] Miguel: for benchmarking we'll instrument both client-side timings and server-side metrics (we provide tracing hooks). typical bench: ramp to target concurrency, hold for 5-10 minutes, capture token/sec and latencies. we also vary batch size and enable/disable prefix caching.
[02:55] Samir: we run our own in-house inference too. curious about comparison — how much better is redwood's runtime vs our current stack per token?
[03:03] Miguel: depends on model and quantization; but across typical open LLMs, our runtime improves tokens/sec by 20-60% via kernel selection, continuous batching, and kv cache management vs vanilla baseline. more concrete numbers in the runbook we'll share.
[03:16] Lena: security is another big factor — we need VPC connectivity, audit logs, and bring-your-own-key (KMS) support. is that all supported?
[03:23] Sofia: yes — Redwood Dedicated includes VPC peering and private endpoints, audit logs, RBAC, and KMS integration for Private deployments. we can share SOC2 report and network diagram.
[03:33] Aisha: perfect. for on-prem we may need an air-gapped option for some merchants — that's a later conversation but good to know it's possible.
[03:41] Miguel: for the benchmark, can you share your test cluster specs? cpu/gpu, network egress, any NAT gateways — that impacts measured p95s.
[03:49] Samir: we'll get that; we have a k8s cluster in GCP, some nodes with T4s but we can provision A100s for test. network egress is 10Gb.
[03:58] Miguel: ideal — we'll coordinate to run on your A100 nodes for apples-to-apples. recommended test plan: small prompt profile first (60 tokens), test 200 -> 1k concurrency, record p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and GPU util. then repeat with streaming session emulation for first-token p95 and sustained tokens/sec.
[04:18] Aisha: how about model variants — do you recommend quantized models to hit our latency? we worry about quality loss for fraud models.
[04:25] Miguel: yes, quantization and model selection are tradeoffs — we can recommend 8-bit quantization profiles that usually preserve classification quality; but we'll include suggested eval prompts to verify. also you can use dedicated for higher precision models if needed.
[04:39] Samir: one practical question: what concurrency limit per connection or per instance? we use connection pooling at the app layer.
[04:45] Miguel: Redwood supports connection-level concurrency knobs; dedicated pools give you predictable per-GPU concurrency. autoscaler policies are configurable — target latency SLOs or target utilization. we can share typical configs.
[05:00] Sofia: quick note on pricing — dedicated is a reserved capacity model (commit), hosted is usage-based. we'll send both options; for your bursty pattern a hybrid dedicated + burst to hosted might be cost-optimal.
[05:13] Lena: that hybrid idea is interesting — ability to burst into hosted when dedicated hits a ceiling. how seamless is fallback?
[05:20] Miguel: we have smart routing and fallback policies — you can route by latency or cost, and automatic fallback to hosted model variants is supported. there is some warmup time but for short bursts it's usually fine.
[05:32] Aisha: regarding metrics, can you surface token-level cost and latency per route in the console? we need to attribute costs per merchant product.
[05:40] Sofia: yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route/model and tracing hooks.
[05:47] Samir: for the benchmark we want to capture end-to-end from service to model to response. do you have a recommended client tool?
[05:53] Miguel: we usually use a benchmark harness (we'll share) that can simulate streaming and non-streaming sessions, vary concurrency, and produce the p50/p95/p99 and token/sec graphs. it emits a CSV/JSON that we can ingest.
[06:05] Aisha: ok good. can you also run a quick whiteboard of expected numbers for a 60-token response on A100 fleet at 200 concurrency? approximate values are fine.
[06:13] Miguel: rough ballpark: with warm cache and tuned batching, 60-token response on A100-class dedicated fleet we expect p50 ~60-80ms, p95 ~120-180ms, tokens/sec per GPU depends on model size but typical token/sec for generation ~300-800 tokens/sec sustained under batching. again depends on model variant and sequence length.
[06:31] Lena: those p95s are within our goal. what about tail behavior at 1k concurrency?
[06:36] Miguel: at 1k bursts—if autoscaler can't spin up fast enough you'll see cold-starts; with reserved burst capacity and appropriate warm pools you can keep p95 <250ms. without reserved capacity it can spike to 400-600ms in hosted during noisy neighbor peaks.
[06:53] Samir: do you provide kernel-level tuning or do we need to handle it?
[06:58] Miguel: Redwood's runtime handles kernel selection and quantization-friendly paths automatically; SEs can recommend config knobs and quant profiles. for private/on-prem there is a bit more ops work but we provide guidance.
[07:10] Aisha: can we get an example of the benchmark CSV and the specific metrics you collect?
[07:16] Miguel: yes we'll attach a sample CSV — it includes timestamp, request id, latency_ms, bytes_in, bytes_out, tokens_in, tokens_out, gpu_util, batch_size, shard_id.
[07:27] Sofia: summary and next steps — we'll send a benchmark plan, sample CSV, pricing, and SOC2 docs; Miguel will propose specific test matrix.
[07:36] Samir: sounds great. timeline — we want results before end of month, is that feasible?
[07:40] Miguel: yes if we run next week we can have initial numbers in 5-7 business days.
[07:46] Lena: final question — any gotchas for streaming where latency looks good but token/sec falls off?
[07:52] Miguel: yes if batch sizes shrink during streaming or kv cache misses happen your tokens/sec can drop; also network jitter increases tail latency. our suggestion: warm caches, keep batch-affinity, and monitor per-shard tail metrics.
[08:05] Aisha: ok let's move to logistics — i'll share the infra details and we'll pick benchmark slots.
[08:11] Sofia: perfect, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the runbook.

[40:00] (wrap-up)
[40:02] Sofia: thanks everyone, recap: Miguel runbook, Sofia pricing + docs, Aisha confirm infra. we'll target bench week of 2026-04-20.
[40:12] Aisha: thanks, talk soon.

Notes on transcription: auto-transcript had a few mis-hearings (K V being spelled out as K V cache, Redwood Dedicated heard as "redwood dedicate" in one spot). Some timestamps approximate.
